source_policy: Public WHO and UNICEF guidance; use as educational context, not diagnosis.

facts: Complementary foods generally begin at 6 months while breastfeeding continues.
Start with small amounts and gradually increase texture, variety, and quantity.
Use responsive feeding: notice hunger and fullness cues, encourage patiently, and do not force-feed.
Offer hygienically prepared food with clean hands and utensils.
WHO guidance describes 2 to 3 meals daily at 6 to 8 months and 3 to 4 meals daily at 9 to 23 months, with nutritious snacks as needed.
Offer family foods in child-sized portions across regular meals and nutritious snacks.
Include a staple such as rice, ragi, dosa, idli, or chapati; a protein food such as dal, green gram, egg, fish, or chicken; and vegetables or fruit.
Milk or curd can be included when tolerated; limit sugary drinks and highly processed snacks.
Serve food in a texture and pieces the child can chew safely, and supervise eating.
Review the child's age, weight, height, appetite, illness history, and growth trend rather than judging from weight alone.
Record weight and height on the growth chart and discuss a concerning trend with an Anganwadi or health worker.
Persistent poor appetite, weight loss, swelling, repeated diarrhoea or vomiting, unusual tiredness, or difficulty breathing needs professional assessment.
Do not prescribe medicines, tonics, or supplements without a qualified health professional.
